result: Loss of Scs2/Scs22 results in dramatic redistribution of Num1 patches from numerous dim and bright patches throughout the cell cortex to predominantly stationary foci at polarized cell ends (bud tip and mother apex), with >70% of scs2/22Δ cells displaying ≤2 bright patches compared to 6% in WT.
evaluation: Claims C3, C49-C57 provide converging evidence from microscopy (Figure 1A, Video 1), quantitative analysis (Figure 1B), and spatial distribution measurements (Figure 1C) demonstrating the redistribution of Num1 upon loss of Scs2/Scs22. The data show both loss of dim patches and reduction in bright patches, with remaining patches localized to cell poles. Controls with single deletions (C54-C57) support specificity and redundancy.

result: Loss of Scs2/22 affects Num1 distribution but not protein stability, as total Num1 levels remain unchanged while individual patch intensity increases 2-3 fold.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 demonstrate through immunoblotting (Figure 1D) and fluorescence quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F) that Num1 protein levels are maintained in scs2/22Δ cells. The increased intensity per patch with fewer total patches indicates redistribution rather than degradation, supporting the conclusion in C61.

result: FRAP analysis shows Num1-GFP patches are stably associated with the cortex in both WT and scs2/22Δ cells, with no fluorescence recovery after photobleaching.
evaluation: Claim C62 presents FRAP data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing no recovery in scs2/22Δ cells. Claims C63-C64 interpret this as stable cortical association, consistent with prior work. The experimental approach is appropriate for assessing protein dynamics at the cortex.

result: Deletion of Scs2/22 causes severe loss of cortical ER without affecting Num1 accumulation timing at the bud tip, while num1Δ does not affect cortical ER.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by ER marker imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B) and time-lapse analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The bidirectional analysis (effect of Scs2/22 on ER and effect of Num1 on ER) strengthens the conclusion that ER loss does not prevent Num1 localization timing.

result: Num1 localization to bud tips in scs2/22Δ cells does not require mitochondria, as disruption of mitochondrial segregation by mmr1Δ or mmr1Δ gem1Δ mutations does not affect Num1-GFP clustering at the bud tip.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 are supported by imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) showing Num1 clustering at bud tips persists even when mitochondrial inheritance is disrupted. This directly contradicts a previous model and establishes mitochondria-independent Num1 localization. The use of two different mitochondrial mutants strengthens the conclusion.

result: Biochemical and colocalization analyses reveal distinct populations of Num1 patches: a pool that co-fractionates with ER in an Scs2/22-dependent manner (77.5% of patches colocalize with Scs2-mRuby2) and a minority population (22.5%) independent of Scs2.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 combine sucrose gradient sedimentation (Figure 1E) and colocalization analysis (Figure 1F) to demonstrate distinct Num1 populations. The quantitative colocalization data using Pearson's correlation coefficients provides rigorous support. The conclusion of distinct populations (C73) is well-justified by the convergent biochemical and imaging evidence.

result: In scs2/22Δ cells, dynein and dynactin localization patterns change with significantly enhanced levels at MT plus ends (consistent with reduced offloading sites) and at cortical foci restricted to bud tip and mother apex, with 2-3 fold higher intensity per focus.
evaluation: Claims C75-C81 present comprehensive imaging and quantification data (Figures 2A-E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B) showing altered dynein/dynactin distribution. The enhanced plus-end signal is logically consistent with fewer cortical offloading sites (C77). Immunoblotting controls (C81) rule out expression changes, supporting redistribution rather than altered protein levels.

result: Dynein targeting mechanisms remain intact in scs2/22Δ cells, with plus-end targeting depending on Pac1/LIS1 and cortical targeting depending on dynactin, despite spatial restriction to cell poles.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 demonstrate through deletion analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) that canonical dynein targeting pathways function normally in scs2/22Δ. This is important for establishing that the observed phenotypes result from altered Num1 distribution rather than general dynein dysfunction.

result: Despite dramatic changes in Num1 distribution, scs2/22Δ cells maintain functional dynein pathway with only 0.7% misoriented spindles (similar to 0.9% in WT), but this requires Num1-dynein interaction as num1LL mutation causes 42.6% misorientation.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 establish a key finding through spindle orientation assays (Figure 2F). The low misorientation rate in scs2/22Δ (C85-C86) contrasts sharply with num1LL scs2/22Δ (C87-C88), demonstrating that residual Num1 patches are sufficient for function. The genetic controls are appropriate and the quantification is robust.

result: Genetic analysis shows scs2/22Δ kar9Δ and scs2/22Δ cin8Δ triple mutants are viable with no growth defects, and no synthetic effect with dyn1Δ, confirming dynein pathway functionality in scs2/22Δ cells.
evaluation: Claims C90-C94 use established genetic interactions (kar9Δ and cin8Δ require functional dynein for viability) to test dynein function. Tetrad dissection data (Table 1) showing viability of triple mutants provides strong genetic evidence supporting the conclusion that dynein pathway remains functional despite altered Num1 distribution.

result: The mechanism of dynein-mediated spindle positioning switches from predominantly MT sliding (86.7% in kar9Δ) to primarily MT capture-shrinkage at the bud tip (77.8% in scs2/22Δ kar9Δ), with the MT plus end staying in contact with Num1 patches during shrinkage.
evaluation: Claims C95-C101 present the central mechanistic finding through time-lapse imaging (Figure 3A-B, Videos 2-3). The quantitative shift in mechanisms is well-documented, and two-color imaging (C97) directly demonstrates MT-Num1 interaction during capture-shrinkage. The 3D imaging (C99) rules out sliding artifacts. This represents a major mechanistic discovery.

result: Dynein persists at shrinking MT plus ends during capture-shrinkage events (15/16 events) and is required for spindle correction, as dyn1Δ completely abolishes correction (0/138 spindles corrected).
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 use kymograph analysis (Figure 3C, Video 4) and deletion analysis (Figure 3B) to demonstrate dynein's role in capture-shrinkage. The high frequency of dynein persistence (15/16) and complete loss of correction in dyn1Δ provide strong evidence for dynein involvement in this mechanism.

result: MT capture-shrinkage at the Num1 site does not require kinesin depolymerases Kip3 or Kar3, as their deletion does not affect capture-shrinkage frequency.
evaluation: Claims C105-C106 use deletion analysis (Figure 3D, Video 5) to rule out alternative mechanisms. This is important for establishing that the observed capture-shrinkage is specifically dynein-dependent rather than mediated by other known MT depolymerases.

result: Cortical anchoring via Num1 is essential for dynein-mediated capture-shrinkage, as num1LL mutation abolishes both capture-shrinkage and spindle correction despite dynein accumulation at MT plus ends, and results in MT lengths equivalent to dyn1Δ.
evaluation: Claims C107-C111 demonstrate through num1LL analysis (Figure 3A-B, Video 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) that cortical anchoring is required for force generation. The observation that MT lengths in num1LL match dyn1Δ (C110) provides additional evidence that anchored dynein acts as a MT destabilizer, supporting the model in C111.

result: Dynein motor activity is required for capture-shrinkage, as dyn1K2424A mutation abolishes spindle correction (0/99) despite prolonged MT attachment at bud tip (3-fold longer duration), with MTs buckling rather than shrinking, suggesting motor activity is needed for MT destabilization or maintaining dynamic cortex-MT connection.
evaluation: Claims C112-C119 use a motor-dead mutant to dissect dynein's role (Figures 3B, 3E, Video 5, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C). The prolonged attachment without productive shrinkage (C115-C117) and buckling phenotype provide strong evidence for motor activity requirement. Claims C118-C119 appropriately present alternative interpretations of the mechanism.

result: The CAP-Gly domain of Nip100/p150Glued is required for persistent MT capture-shrinkage at the bud tip, as its deletion dramatically reduces capture-shrinkage frequency and shortens MT-bud tip interaction duration (55.2±7.2s vs 111.2±12.1s) without affecting MT stability or Nip100 expression.
evaluation: Claims C120-C129 present a mechanistic dissection of dynactin's role using CAP-Gly domain deletion (Figures 4B-E, Video 6). The reduced interaction duration (C128) without effects on MT length (C124-C125) or protein stability (C126-C127) supports the specific role of CAP-Gly in tethering. The interpretation (C129) is well-supported by the data.

result: CAP-Gly deletion does not affect dynein localization to MT plus ends or cortex, or the amount of dynein per cortical focus, ruling out anchoring defects as the cause of reduced capture-shrinkage.
evaluation: Claims C130-C132 provide important controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C) showing that CAP-Gly deletion specifically affects MT tethering rather than dynein recruitment. This strengthens the conclusion that CAP-Gly functions in maintaining MT-cortex connections during shrinkage.

result: Loss of both dynein pulling mechanisms (CAP-Gly deletion disrupting capture-shrinkage plus scs2/22Δ disrupting sliding) results in additive defects, with significantly enhanced spindle misalignment (47.2% vs 35.7%) and severe synthetic viability defects.
evaluation: Claims C133-C135 demonstrate genetic interaction between the two mechanisms through spindle alignment assays (Figure 4F) and growth assays (Figure 4G). The additive phenotypes provide strong evidence that capture-shrinkage and sliding represent distinct, complementary mechanisms for dynein-mediated spindle positioning.

result: CAAX-targeted Num1 rescues lateral patch distribution and MT sliding mechanism in scs2/22Δ cells, with 80% of corrections via sliding (vs 22.2% with native Num1), more oblique MT-cortex angles (54.0° vs 83.7°), and spatial correlation of mechanism with Num1 position along bud cortex.
evaluation: Claims C137-C145 present a key rescue experiment (Figures 5A-D, Video 7) demonstrating that Num1 spatial distribution determines pulling mechanism. The quantitative shift in mechanisms (C139), angle measurements (C140), and spatial correlation analysis (C142-C143) provide strong support for the conclusion that Scs2/22's primary role is distributing Num1 for MT sliding (C145).

result: Lateral Num1 patches enhance nuclear migration efficiency, as scs2/22Δ kar9Δ shows reduced spindle movement frequency (11.2% vs 22.5%) and shorter penetration distance, both rescued by Num1-GFP-CAAX, independent of MT dynamics changes.
evaluation: Claims C146-C151 quantify the functional importance of lateral patches using HU-arrested cells (Figures 5E-F, Table 2). The rescue by CAAX-Num1 (C149-C150) and control for MT dynamics (C148) support the conclusion that lateral patches specifically enhance migration efficiency (C151). The statistical analysis is appropriate.

result: Bni1 formin is required for Num1 localization at the bud tip (72.3% to 33.3% upon deletion) and shows synergistic spindle misalignment with scs2/22Δ (64.3% in double mutant vs 19.5% in bni1Δ alone), but this is independent of F-actin as latrunculin A does not affect Num1 localization.
evaluation: Claims C154-C160 identify Bni1's role through deletion analysis (Figures 6A-C, Video 8) and latrunculin A treatment (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The synergistic phenotype (C156-C157) and F-actin independence (C158-C159) support the conclusion that Bni1 itself, not its actin nucleation activity, is required (C160).

result: In WT cells, MT sliding is terminated by capture-shrinkage at the bud tip in ~49% of events, with the MT plus end encountering Num1 patches and undergoing depolymerization while attached, and bni1Δ increases oversliding frequency, suggesting capture-shrinkage regulates spindle movement.
evaluation: Claims C164-C170 demonstrate that both mechanisms operate in WT cells through time-lapse imaging (Figure 7A-C, Videos 9-12). The colocalization with Num1 (C165), straightening during depolymerization (C166-C167), and increased oversliding in bni1Δ (C169) provide converging evidence for the regulatory model (C170).

result: The spatial distribution of Num1 determines dynein pulling mechanism: restriction to bud tip limits dynein to MT end interactions enabling capture-shrinkage, while lateral distribution allows MT lattice interactions enabling sliding, with bud tip Num1 functioning as a brake to prevent oversliding and ensure proper spindle positioning.
evaluation: Claims C171-C180 synthesize the major findings into a comprehensive model presented in the Discussion. The model is well-supported by the experimental data showing mechanism switching (C171-C176), coupling of mechanisms (C177), Bni1 dependence (C178), and the brake function (C179-C180). This represents the paper's central conceptual advance.

result: Cortical ER has a facilitative role in dynein pathway by anchoring Num1 at ER-PM junctions to enable MT sliding, as evidenced by dim patches along lateral bud cortex in WT, their loss in scs2/22Δ, reduced sliding events, and decreased spindle penetration distance.
evaluation: Claims C181, C193-C198 integrate multiple lines of evidence (Figures 1A, 5—figure supplement 2A-B) to support ER's facilitative role. The correlation between dim patches and sliding (C193-C195), reduced effectiveness of remaining sliding (C196), and interpretation of penetration distance (C198) support the model, though alternative mechanisms are appropriately acknowledged (C197).

result: Dynein pulling forces are spatially regulated by two distinct Num1 populations: Scs2/22-dependent lateral patches initiate and facilitate MT sliding, while bud tip Num1 terminates sliding by capturing MT plus ends and inducing catastrophe, providing temporal control over spindle movement.
evaluation: Claims C199-C204 present the paper's overarching conclusion about spatial regulation of dynein. This synthesis is well-supported by the cumulative experimental evidence showing distinct populations (C199-C201) and their regulatory roles (C202-C204). The model integrates findings about ER barrier function with the new capture-shrinkage mechanism.
